paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.heading: Pinewood Lodge
paragraphs.text: Sleeps up to six in three bedrooms. Five minutes' walk from the lake, with its own private garden and barbecue. Pets are welcome for a small extra charge. Minimum stay: one week in July and August; three nights at other times. Wi-Fi is available in the main living area only.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.heading: The Boathouse
paragraphs.text: A one-bedroom apartment built directly over the water, ideal for couples. Guests have free use of a rowing boat and life jackets. Not suitable for children under twelve because of the open balcony. The nearest shop is a 20-minute drive away, so a car is essential.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.heading: Harbour View Apartments
paragraphs.text: Four modern apartments, each sleeping four, located in the centre of Arden village above the harbour café. Shops, restaurants and the bus station are all within walking distance. Guests receive a 10% discount on meals in the café. Parking is limited to one space per apartment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.heading: Willow Barn
paragraphs.text: A converted farm building sleeping eight, set in fields two kilometres from the village. Fully accessible for wheelchair users, with a ground-floor bedroom and wet room. Bicycles can be hired from the owners, who live on the same farm. Short breaks of two nights are available all year round.

Membership of Arden Public Library is free for anyone who lives, works or studies in the district. To join, bring proof of address such as a recent utility bill; a driving licence alone is not accepted. Visitors to the area may take out temporary membership for £5, which allows them to borrow two items at a time.

Full members may borrow up to twelve books for three weeks. Items can be renewed twice online or by phone, unless another member has reserved them. DVDs and audiobooks are loaned for one week and cost £1 per item.

Late returns are charged at 20p per item per day, up to a maximum of £5 per item. Children's books are exempt from late charges. If an item is lost or damaged, you will be asked to pay for a replacement.

Members can use the library computers free of charge for up to two hours a day. Printing costs 10p per page for black and white and 50p for colour. The library also offers free one-to-one sessions for people who want help using email or online services; these must be booked in advance.

The library is open from 9 am to 7 pm on weekdays and from 10 am to 4 pm on Saturdays. It is closed on Sundays and public holidays. A book return box outside the main entrance can be used at any time.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Working in a busy hospital can be rewarding, but it is also physically and emotionally demanding. Recent staff surveys showed that more than a third of employees had considered leaving their job because of stress. The Staff Wellbeing Programme was launched last year in response to these findings, with the aim of supporting staff in all departments, not just those in clinical roles.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: At the heart of the programme is a confidential counselling service. Any member of staff can arrange up to six free sessions with a qualified counsellor, either face to face or by video call. Managers are not informed when an employee uses the service, and sessions can be scheduled outside working hours if preferred.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Because many of our staff work night shifts, we have extended the opening hours of the staff restaurant, which now serves hot meals until 2 am. Healthy options are clearly labelled and are sold at a reduced price. Free fruit is also available in every staff room.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Physical activity is encouraged through a range of subsidised schemes. Staff can join the local leisure centre at half the normal membership fee, and a 'cycle to work' scheme allows employees to buy a bicycle and spread the cost over twelve months through their salary.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: We recognise that long shifts can make it difficult to balance work with family life. Employees with caring responsibilities may request flexible working arrangements, such as compressed hours or a fixed shift pattern. All requests are considered, although they cannot always be granted where they would affect patient care.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The programme is reviewed every six months by a committee that includes staff representatives from each department. Suggestions for improvements can be submitted through the wellbeing page of the staff intranet, and the most popular ideas are trialled the following year.

texts.title: How to Write a Site Incident Report

paragraphs.text: An incident report must be completed whenever an accident, injury or dangerous occurrence happens on site. The report should be written by the supervisor in charge of the area at the time, not by the injured person, and submitted within 24 hours.

Begin by recording the basic facts: the date, time and exact location, and the names of everyone involved. Witnesses should be asked to give their own written statements, which are attached to the report. Avoid giving your opinion at this stage; the purpose of the report is to describe what happened, not to decide who was responsible.

Next, describe the sequence of events in plain language. Photographs are extremely useful and should be taken before anything is moved, unless doing so would put someone at risk. Include details of the weather and lighting if these may have been a factor.

Finally, list the immediate actions taken, such as first aid given or equipment taken out of service. The safety manager will then carry out an investigation, normally within five working days, to identify the root cause and recommend measures to prevent a similar incident.

texts.title: The Box That Changed the World

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few inventions have reshaped the global economy as profoundly as the shipping container, yet few are so rarely noticed. The standard steel box, usually twenty or forty feet long, is now so familiar that it is easy to forget that, until the 1950s, almost all cargo was loaded onto ships piece by piece. Sacks of coffee, barrels of oil and crates of machinery were carried up gangways by teams of dock workers, a process that could keep a ship in port for a week or more.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The man usually credited with changing this was Malcolm McLean, an American trucking businessman. Frustrated by the hours his drivers spent waiting at ports, McLean reasoned that it would be faster to lift an entire truck trailer onto a ship than to unload its contents. In 1956 he converted an old tanker, the Ideal X, to carry fifty-eight containers from New Jersey to Texas. The voyage is often described as the birth of containerization, although similar ideas had been tested in Europe and elsewhere decades earlier.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: McLean's real achievement was not the box itself but the system around it. He realised that the container would only save money if ships, cranes, trucks and trains were all designed to handle it. His company developed specialised cranes, as well as ships with cells that held containers securely, and it calculated that loading costs fell from nearly six dollars a ton to just sixteen cents.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Standardisation proved to be the greatest obstacle. In the early 1960s, different shipping lines used containers of different sizes, which meant that a box from one company could not be carried on another company's ship. It took years of negotiation, led by the International Organization for Standardization, before common dimensions and corner fittings were agreed in the late 1960s. Once these standards were in place, containers could move seamlessly between ships, trains and lorries anywhere in the world.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The consequences for port cities were dramatic. Container ships require deep water and vast areas of flat land for storing boxes, which many traditional harbours in city centres could not provide. As a result, activity moved to new terminals, often many kilometres away. In London, Liverpool and New York, historic docks closed within a generation, and tens of thousands of dock workers lost their jobs. Some of these areas remained derelict for years before being redeveloped as housing and offices.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For manufacturers, by contrast, the container opened up new possibilities. Because transport became cheaper and more reliable, companies could produce components in one country, assemble them in another and sell the finished goods worldwide. Economists have estimated that containerization did more to increase international trade in the late twentieth century than all the trade agreements of the period combined.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The container has also created new challenges. Because sealed boxes are rarely opened during their journey, customs officials can inspect only a small percentage of them, which makes the system attractive to smugglers. Thousands of containers are also lost at sea each year, usually during storms, and those that float just below the surface pose a danger to smaller vessels.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Today, the largest container ships can carry more than twenty thousand containers, and shipping companies continue to order even bigger vessels. Some analysts, however, question whether this trend can continue. Very large ships can only enter a limited number of ports, and when one is delayed, the effects are felt throughout the global supply chain, as was shown in 2021 when a single ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days.
